beads.title: tnet down carries neither of Go's two down behaviours: --reason and the lose-SSH refusal
beads.description: Go's `down` is not a bare verb. `newDownFlagSet` registers `--reason` ("reason for the disconnect, if required by a policy"), which `runDown` attaches to the prefs edit as `apitype.RequestReasonKey` so a tailnet whose policy demands a justification gets one; and it calls `registerAcceptRiskFlag`, so `runDown` refuses when `isSSHOverTailscale()` — disconnecting over a Tailscale SSH session drops that very session — unless `--accept-risk=lose-ssh` (or `all`) was passed. `tnet down` is a fieldless `Command::Down` that dispatches `Request::Down`: it takes neither flag, applies no risk gate, and a `tailscale down --reason "maintenance"` copied from a runbook exits 2 at argument parsing. Both halves already exist in this fork and would be reused rather than invented — `--reason` is already on `tnet logout` (carried to the daemon and logged locally), and the `lose-ssh` risk refusal plus `is_ssh_over_tailscale` already gate `up --force-reauth`. Port the error paths with the flags: Go returns `too many non-flag arguments: %q` on a stray positional, and when the backend is already `Stopped` it prints "Tailscale was already stopped." to stderr and exits 0 rather than issuing a redundant edit. Decide whether `--reason` on `down` reaches the daemon the way `logout --reason` does, or is recorded locally only.

beads.title: tnet exit-node list has no --filter, and no country/city data to filter on
beads.description: Go's `exit-node list` prints five columns — IP, HOSTNAME, COUNTRY, CITY, STATUS — after running peers through `filterFormatAndSortExitNodes`, which groups by country then city, keeps only the highest-priority node per city, synthesises an "Any" city row for multi-city countries, and honours `--filter` ("filter exit nodes by country"). This fork's `format_exit_node_list` prints IP + hostname + an online marker, because `PeerReport` (src/localapi.rs) carries no `Location`: the engine surfaces no per-peer country/city/priority from the netmap, so there is nothing to group by and nothing for `--filter` to match. That makes the column set and the flag engine-gated, and an engine ask for peer `Location` is the honest first step. Two error paths are daemon-buildable today and diverge right now: Go returns the error `no exit nodes found` (non-zero exit) when no peer advertises a default route, where this fork prints "(no exit nodes available in this tailnet)" and exits 0; and Go returns `no exit nodes found for %q` when a filter matches nothing. Go also refuses a stray positional with `unexpected non-flag arguments to 'tailscale exit-node list'`.

beads.title: tnet bugreport has no --diagnose and no --record
beads.description: Go's `bugreport` takes two flags this fork does not model. `--diagnose` ("run additional in-depth checks") sets `local.BugReportOpts.Diagnose`, so the daemon runs an extra diagnostic pass and logs it alongside the marker. `--record` is CLI choreography: it starts the bugreport request on a goroutine with a `Record` done-channel, prints "Recording started; please reproduce your issue and then press Enter...", blocks on stdin, closes the channel, and then prints the marker plus "Please provide both bugreport markers above to the support team or GitHub issue." — so the operator hands over a before/after pair bracketing the reproduction. `tnet bugreport` accepts only the optional positional note. `--record` needs nothing from the engine: it is two `BugReport` round-trips around a stdin wait, and this fork's marker is already a local identifier. `--diagnose` needs a diagnostic pass on the daemon side and a decision about what belongs in it, given this fork uploads no logs — the marker is local, so "in-depth checks" must mean something the operator can read, not something support fetches. Port Go's argument refusal too: more than one positional is `unknown arguments`.

beads.title: tnet lock init's argument grammar means something different from Go's
beads.description: Go's `lock init` is `tailscale lock init [--gen-disablement-for-support] --gen-disablements N <trusted-key>...`: the positionals are the tailnet-lock public keys initially trusted to sign nodes, the CLI *mints* the disablement secrets itself (`--gen-disablements`, default 1) and prints them once with "they WILL NOT be shown again", `--gen-disablement-for-support` adds one more that is transmitted to Tailscale, and `--confirm` gates the whole thing: without it the command prints the trusted keys and the exact re-run command and exits without doing anything. It also refuses up front if the current node's own lock key is not among the trusted keys ("the tailnet lock key of the current node must be one of the trusted keys during initialization") and if the lock is already on ("tailnet lock is already enabled"). This fork's `tnet lock init` takes a single positional `<DISABLEMENT-SECRET>` and forwards it as `Request::LockInit { secret_hex }`, because the engine's `Device::tka_init` accepts exactly one `disablement_secret: Vec<u8>` and no key list. Same command name, incompatible argument meaning: `tnet lock init tlpub:...` does not fail, it treats a public key as a disablement secret. Needs an engine ask extending #17/#25 to take a trusted-key set and multiple disablement values; the `--confirm` two-step and the two refusals are CLI-side and can land with it.

beads.title: tnet ping takes an IP where Go takes a hostname, and has none of Go's ping-type selectors
beads.description: Go's `ping <hostname-or-IP>` resolves its argument through `tailscaleIPFromArg`: a literal IP is used as-is, otherwise it matches the peer list by MagicDNS name and falls back to the host resolver, and a match against self prints `%v is local Tailscale IP` and exits 0. It then carries `--verbose` (which logs the `lookup %q => %q` resolution), `-c` (max pings, 0 for infinity), `--timeout`, `--until-direct`, `--size` ("size of the ping message (disco pings only)") and three type selectors that pick `tailcfg.PingType` — `--tsmp`, `--icmp`, `--peerapi`, defaulting to disco — where `--peerapi` prints a different line entirely (`hit peerapi of %s (%s) at %s in %s`) and tsmp/icmp return after the first pong. `tnet ping` takes `IP` only, plus `--count`/`--timeout`/`--until-direct`/`--no-until-direct`, so `tnet ping my-laptop` fails and none of the four probe shapes exist. Split the work honestly: the argument resolution, `--verbose`, and Go's two terminal refusals (`no reply`, and `direct connection not established` when `--until-direct` ran out of attempts) are daemon-buildable now; `--size` and the type selectors are engine-gated, since `Device::ping`/`ping_disco` do a disco probe returning a `Duration` with no size knob and no TSMP/ICMP/peerAPI path — file the engine ask rather than faking them.

beads.title: tnet whois has no --proto, and does not take Go's ip[:port] argument
beads.description: Go's `whois` is `tailscale whois [--json] ip[:port]` and calls `localClient.WhoIsProto(ctx, whoIsArgs.proto, args[0])`, where `--proto` is documented as `protocol; one of "tcp" or "udp"; empty means both`. That is not cosmetic: a whois is a *flow* lookup, so the same address and port can belong to different sessions depending on protocol, and an empty proto asks for either. This fork's `tnet whois` takes a bare `IP` positional and a `--json` flag, and its `Request::Whois { ip }` has no protocol field, so a `tailscale whois --proto=tcp 100.64.0.9:22` copied from Go dies at argument parsing and there is no way to disambiguate a flow. Decide whether the LocalAPI verb grows a proto field (and whether the engine's whois lookup can honour one at all, which is the part to check before promising it) or whether the flag is accepted and refused by name the way `set --sync` now is. Port Go's two argument refusals with it: `too many arguments, expected at most one peer` and `missing argument, expected one peer`. Note this is the *request* half — the already-documented deviation that `WhoisReport.user` is always empty is the response half and is a separate concern.

beads.title: tnet dns status has no --all, and prints the advanced sections unconditionally
beads.description: Go's `dns status` is `tailscale dns status [--all] [--json]`, and `--all` is what gates the advanced half of the human output: `formatDNSStatusText(data, all)` prints fallback resolvers, nameservers, certificate domains, extra records and the exit-node filtered set only when it is set, and the short form otherwise. This fork's `tnet dns status` takes `--json` only, so `dns status --all` from a Go runbook exits 2 at argument parsing. The awkward part is that the fork is *more* verbose than Go by default rather than less: `DnsStatusReport` already carries `fallback_resolvers`, `cert_domains`, `extra_records` and `exit_node_filtered_set`, and `format_dns_status` prints all of them every time. So this is not an engine gap at all — the work is to add the flag, move those sections behind it, and keep the default output to Go's short form. The two genuine reductions here stay as they are and stay documented: the "Use Tailscale DNS" accept-dns line and the system-DNS section (Go's `GetDNSOSConfig`, including its `not supported on this platform` fallback) have no counterpart in this build.

beads.title: tnet web has no --cgi and no --origin, so a reverse-proxied deployment cannot state its origin
beads.description: Go's `web` registers five flags: `--listen`, `--prefix`, `--readonly`, `--cgi` ("run as CGI script") and `--origin` ("origin at which the web UI is served (if behind a reverse proxy or used with cgi)"). `--cgi` changes the whole serving model — `runWeb` sets `CGIMode`, serves via `cgi.Serve(webServer)` instead of binding a listener, and skips the tailscaled-shutdown path it takes in listener mode — while `--origin` sets `OriginOverride` so the UI emits correct absolute URLs when the address it is reached at is not the address it bound. This fork's `tnet web` has `--listen`/`--prefix`/`--readonly`/`--no-browser` and always runs its own listener, so a `tnet web --cgi --origin=https://ts.example.com/tailscale` from a Go deployment dies at the parser and there is no way to tell the UI what URL it is really served at — `--prefix` alone fixes paths but not scheme or host. Decide whether CGI is in scope for a daemon this fork's shape (it is a real serving mode, not a flag rename) or whether it is refused by name, and either way `--origin` is small and worth having on its own: this fork's UI is read-only, so the origin only affects link generation.

beads.title: tailnetd --tun is an unknown argument, where Go's daemon takes the flag every unit file passes
beads.description: Go's daemon registers `--tun` as `tunnel interface name; use "userspace-networking" (beta) to not use TUN`, and it is the single most-copied flag on the tailscaled command line: packaged systemd units, container entrypoints and cloud images all pass `--tun=userspace-networking` or `--tun=tailscale0`. This fork deliberately made TUN a *pref* instead (`tnet up --tun`/`--tun-name`/`--tun-mtu`, persisted in `Prefs::tun_enabled`), and records that decision in the rustdoc on `tailnetd`'s flag struct — but the flag itself is simply absent, so `tailnetd --tun=userspace-networking` dies with clap's "unexpected argument" before the daemon starts. That is exactly the failure shape #302 fixed for `--bird-socket`, and the same three answers apply: accept it and map `--tun=<name>`/`userspace-networking` onto the existing pref, accept it and refuse by name with a message that points at `tnet up --tun`, or leave it unknown and stop calling the deviation documented. Whichever is chosen, decide it for `--tun` alone or for the whole cluster, since Go's related `--statedir`/`--state` interaction differs; note `--state` is already tracked separately.

beads.title: tailnetd has no --encrypt-state or --hardware-attestation, and no recorded state-at-rest decision
beads.description: Go's daemon takes two TPM-backed flags this fork has neither implemented nor ruled on. `--encrypt-state` encrypts the state file on disk (TPM on Linux and Windows; unsupported elsewhere) and, when unset, turns itself on if the platform supports it or if the syspolicy key `EncryptState` asks for it. `--hardware-attestation` binds the node identity to hardware-backed keys (TPM 2.0, SecureEnclave, Keystore), likewise defaulting from the `HardwareAttestation` policy key. `handleTPMFlags` carries the interesting part — the refusals: an explicit `--hardware-attestation` on an unsupported build is `log.Fatal("--hardware-attestation is not supported on this platform or in this build of tailscaled")`, and it is additionally refused against a portable state store because TPM-bound keys cannot be migrated between machines; a policy that requires it on a device that cannot do it logs `[unexpected] policy requires hardware attestation...` and continues. This fork stores the node and WireGuard keys unencrypted under a 0700 state dir — `THREAT_MODEL.md` states that plainly as a trust boundary, but nowhere is it recorded as a parity *decision*, and both flags are unknown arguments today. This fork now has a syspolicy layer with a real file source, so the policy-key half is reachable; decide adopt-vs-out-of-scope, and make the daemon say which.

beads.title: tailnetd has no debug subcommand, so Go's daemon-side network diagnostics have no counterpart
beads.description: Go's daemon takes a `debug` *subcommand* — `tailscaled debug` with its own flag set — that runs standalone, without a running daemon or a LocalAPI socket: `--ifconfig` dumps the netmon network state once as JSON, `--monitor` runs the network monitor forever printing every link change, `--derp <region>` tests a DERP ping via the named region code, `--get-url <url>` fetches a URL with an httptrace, and `--portmap` runs port-mapping (NAT-PMP/PCP/UPnP) debugging. This is the tool you reach for when the node will not come up at all, which is precisely when `tnet debug` (which needs the daemon) cannot help. `tailnetd` has no subcommands whatsoever, so `tailnetd debug --monitor` is a clap error; its own `--debug` flag is an unrelated thing, the listen address of the debug-metrics HTTP server. Scope it against what already exists: this daemon has a link monitor (`src/ipn/linkmon.rs`) that `--ifconfig`/`--monitor` could render, while `--derp` needs a DERP client the daemon does not own and `--portmap` needs the port mapper that does not exist in the engine at all. Port Go's two refusals: a stray positional is `unknown non-flag debug subcommand arguments`, and no recognised flag at all is an error, not a no-op. Distinct from the CLI-side `tnet debug` verb backlog.

beads.title: The --config loader has drifted from ipn.ConfigVAlpha and from this fork's own prefs
beads.description: `src/conffile.rs` mirrors Go's `ipn.ConfigVAlpha` and deliberately does NOT reject unknown keys (forward-compat), leaning instead on `warn_unmapped` to surface anything parsed-but-unhonoured. That contract has two holes now. First, four Go fields are in neither the struct nor the warning list, so they are silently dropped: `AdvertiseExitNode`, `RemoteConfig`, `RelayServerPort` and `RelayServerStaticEndpoints`. `AdvertiseExitNode` is the damaging one — it is not engine-gated at all, this fork has `Prefs::advertise_exit_node` and `tnet up --advertise-exit-node`, so a Go config declaring `"AdvertiseExitNode": true` boots a node that quietly is not an exit node and says nothing. Note Go's `ToPrefs` also *composes* it with `AdvertiseRoutes` (it appends the two default routes rather than replacing the set), so a faithful port has to get that ordering right. Second, the drift runs the other way too: `warn_unmapped` still reports `AllowLANWhileUsingExitNode`, `OperatorUser`, `PostureChecking` and `RunWebClient` as unmapped after the prefs behind them shipped, and `apply_to_prefs` maps none of the eight newer prefs (`--operator`, `--nickname`, `--report-posture`, `--webclient`, `--auto-update`/`--update-check`, `--advertise-connector`, `--exit-node-allow-lan-access`), so the declarative path is strictly weaker than the flag path for prefs the daemon already has. Re-derive the struct field-by-field against `ipn/conf.go`, map what this fork can honour, and warn for the rest.
